rows.evidence: Q1: Section III (Implementation and Testing) and IV (Results) report the authors' own calibration experiments (Tables I-III, Figs 5-6) and a 19 April-3 May 2016 evaluation experiment in three clay-filled containers comparing sensor readings against gravimetric weight measurements (Tables IV-VII).
rows.notes: The study only evaluates the measurement accuracy of low-cost resistive soil moisture sensors (calibration curves, percent error against gravimetric ground truth, sources of error such as corrosion, ion concentration, temperature, installation). It reports no result on water conservation or irrigation water efficiency, no irrigation scheduling trial, and no data on farmer accessibility or cost-effectiveness in developing regions; the low-cost/developing-country point appears only as motivation in the Introduction. Its own finding is actually negative for the claimed precondition: average percent error above 10% is judged unacceptable, and the sensors are not recommended for continuous monitoring or high-accuracy irrigation control, only for short-term dry/humid indication. Sensor accuracy is at most a precondition for precision-irrigation water savings, hence upstream.

notes: Full text appears complete (conference paper, five sections plus references). The claim concerns water-efficiency gains from affordable sensors; the study addresses only sensor accuracy in a container experiment with one clay soil and three sensor units, with no crop, field, or water-use measurement.
